newsitem.title: USA: Red River rises again at Fargo, levees weaken.
newsitem.headline: Red River rises again at Fargo, levees weaken.

text.p: The Red River surprised forecasters on Monday by rising again to hit a new crest in Fargo, and city officials put out a call for volunteers to shore up levees holding back icy waters.

Warmer spring weather melting a winter's accumulation of snow added to the runoff, as did a break in a dike along a tributary of the Red south of Fargo. The river rose to 37.8 feet (11.52 metres) on Monday, topping Saturday's crest of 37.6 feet (11.46 metres), after a slight drop on Sunday that forecasters had expected to continue.
Both readings are more than 20 feet (6.09 metres) over flood stage and the highest recorded since a destructive flood of 1897.
A call went out on Monday afternoon for 200 sandbag volunteers in Fargo to shore up vulnerable spots, and officials upstream in Breckenridge, Minnesota, were also appealing for sandbagging help.

There was more bad news on Monday with a decision to start releasing water from Lake Traverse, a reservoir on the Minnesota-South Dakota border that empties into the Boise de Sioux River, a tributary of the Red. The lake reservoir is full and hydrologists said they had no choice.
The release will send more more water to the Red River Valley and could cause problems for the Breckenridge area.

At Gardner, North Dakota, a crossroads village north of Fargo, residents lost a fight to save Nora Church, a 1913 edifice founded by one of the oldest Norwegian Lutheran congregations in the state. They opened basement windows to let floodwaters in after moving possessions upstairs.
The nearby graveyard was under water.
"Right now we don't really anticipate any significant drop in the river for three or four days," Dennis Walaker, director of operations at the Fargo Public Works Department, said.

The Sheyenne River, which feeds into the Red north of Fargo, burst through dikes south of the city this weekend, merging with the Wild Rice River, which flows into the Red south of Fargo. Earthen and sandbag dikes built as temporary barriers to hold back the water will be tested longer than expected, Walaker said.

Donald Schwert, a geologist at North Dakota State University in Fargo, said a number of similar "surges" may be expected in the coming days. "There's so much water south of us and warmer weather has released a lot of water that had been locked up in ice and snow," he said. "And we have ice jams" that back water up.

Residents fled some towns north of Fargo in anticipation of flooding along the Red and its tributaries as high water drains north toward Canada. Emergency crews said ice on the Red slowed its flow north, backing water into tributaries and creating additional flooding along these waterways.
